accuracy.evidence: Checked against the PSHE Association Programme of Study for PSHE education (KS3 core themes Relationships and Living in the wider world: managing peer influence, assertiveness, recognising and challenging coercion and manipulation) and the DfE statutory Relationships, Sex and Health Education guidance (respectful relationships; consent as a free choice that can be withdrawn). The four styles match their sources: directive/autocratic and democratic from Lewin, Lippitt & White (1939), servant leadership from Greenleaf (1970), transformational from Burns (1978) and Bass (1985); 'the right style depends on the situation' follows Hersey & Blanchard's situational leadership. No claim is made that one style is best overall. Numeric items n−2, n*t, y−p and n−q stay positive at every parameter corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the common teen beliefs named in PSHE Association guidance on leadership and peer influence: one style is always right (step 1 prediction options 'Democratic: always ask everyone' and 'Directive: someone must be in charge', m1), loud equals knowledgeable (step 3 prediction, tag loud), 'any other ideas?' counts as inclusion (lab button and tag room), threats and public shaming as 'being firm' (team meters, tag firm, m6), fake social proof and requests for secrecy not seen as manipulation (sort step, tags crowd and secret, m3), and a pressured yes counted as consent (tags said and small, m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaglead combines style recognition from a leader's own words, style-to-situation matching, a seated meeting where quiet members are invited by name and each reveals an idea nobody had heard, a persuasion-versus-pressure sort, and a team problem round with live trust and effort meters that move differently for inspiring, threatening, shaming, tricking, pulling rank or bribing. It differs from flagroles (Roles in a Group: handing out leader, ideas, supporter and mediator badges), flagpeer (resisting peer pressure as the target) and flagassert (communication style slider and I-statements). The gate reports under 30% shingle overlap with every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner meets each idea through a consequence: wrong style picks for a fire alarm or a stuck teammate get the reason the style fails there; asking the room 'Any other ideas?' produces nothing, while asking Priya, Ben and Lena by name reveals the three best stall ideas; sorting six lines shows the common thread (free to say no); and in the team round a threat raises effort while trust drops by 25, so the learner sees why coercion is a poor long-term strategy before the text says so.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves. 'Democratic: always' and 'Directive: always' fail in step 2 when each of the four situations needs a different style. 'Yes: they talk most because they know most' fails when the three quiet members supply the strongest ideas. 'It stays the same: results are what count' fails when the trust meter falls after a threat even as effort rises. Task completion echoes the locked-in choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with two wrong options each, every one with its own message: vote (a vote takes time in danger), slow (asking about needs suits someone stuck, not an evacuation), loud (talking most is not knowing most), room (open questions get the same confident voices), reason (a threat gives no reason), firm (firm is clear; threatening exclusion is coercion), crowd (fake 'everyone agreed'), secret (secrecy from trusted adults is a warning sign), said (a yes from fear is not free), small (size does not matter), orders (that is directive) and loose (hands-off with no shared goal). In-lab wrong choices also name the slip (e.g. 'Picking the person who cannot say no is using power, not leading').

readability.evidence: learn/validate_lessons.py passes the learner limits (kid ≤ 6.5, adult ≤ 9.5); the adult text was rewritten after a first draft read at FK grade 16.1. Kid paragraphs define each style in one sentence and give one everyday example (fire drill, class trip, stuck friend). Lab lines are short quoted speech, and canvas labels are short ('Quiet voices heard: 2 of 3', 'Trust: 65').

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each step has one job (name styles, fit style to moment, include quiet voices, persuasion vs pressure, consequences of coercion). Feedback lines give a reason, and item explanations say why the answer is right and what the wrong idea gets wrong.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px (Android profile) in light and dark, before and after Show me for every step. The first pass had the 'Quiet voices heard' line overlapping the two lower seats and the problem text squeezed onto one line in the team step; the seating ellipse was raised and flattened and the problem now wraps onto two lines, then re-checked. Style boxes sit in a 2 × 2 grid, the six speech lines wrap inside the card, and the long team-choice buttons wrap below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: the four style buttons (aria-label 'Servant style'), 'Ask Priya by name' for each person, 'Ask the whole room for other ideas', 'Go round the circle', the two sort buttons and the three team choices. After each action the canvas aria-label reads the result and state, e.g. 'You asked Lena by name. Lena: “Ask the art club to make the signs.” … Quiet voices heard: 3 of 3.' and 'Trust 65, effort 60.' Challenge feedback is an aria-live status. walk.cjs reports axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors; a scripted run pressing every wrong option raised no errors.
